title: Sheikh Farid of Pakpattan
hookLine: Baba Farid, a Chishti Sufi of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, whose Punjabi verses the Gurus treasured

cards: It's still dark. A man gets up, washes his hands, face and feet, and stands to pray before the light comes.
Then he says something about himself, plainly, for anyone to hear: this path is hard, and I keep walking the world's way instead.
That's the voice of Sheikh Farid, a Sufi, a Muslim mystic of the Chishti order, whom tradition places at Pakpattan, in the Punjab, before the time of the Gurus.

teach.h: FARIDA — TAPPING HIMSELF ON THE SHOULDER.
teach.b: We met Farid in year one, when his verses came into the Guru's keeping. Today, listen to how he talks to himself.
His saloks in the Guru Granth Sahib often open with his own name, Farida, as if he's tapping himself on the shoulder.
One, on Ang 1381, in paraphrase: rise, Farid, make your ablutions and offer your morning prayer. The head that doesn't bow to the Master, cut it off and set it aside.
That's the language of a Sufi's day: wudu, the washing before prayer, and namaz, the prayer itself. It's blunt, but Farid isn't threatening anyone.
A head that won't bow isn't worth carrying: a life without bowing is missing its point. Then the honest salok, from the same pages.

In paraphrase: the dervish's door is a hard path, and I walk the way the world walks. I've tied up a bundle and lifted it onto my head; where can I go and throw it down? A dervish is a Sufi who has given up the world.

teach.h: A BUNDLE HE CAN'T PUT DOWN.
teach.b: Farid, a revered Sufi, admits he's carrying a bundle he can't put down. Hold those two together: get up and bow; and this is hard, and I'm not there. Some readers hear in that why the Gurus kept his words.
He doesn't pretend. He speaks in Punjabi, the speech a farmer or a weaver could follow.
And there's a quiet gift on the page: a Muslim's reminder to rise for morning prayer, kept and sung in the Sikh scripture, in his own words.
Farid's verses belong to Sikh devotion, and Farid remains a Sufi of the Punjab.

how: Sheikh Farid's hymns and saloks are part of the Guru Granth Sahib and are sung in kirtan and read in gurdwaras with the rest of Gurbani; Farid is also honored by Muslims in the Punjab, and his shrine is in Pakpattan.

games.q: you're a respected Sufi, and people come to you for guidance. you write a verse about your own path. what do you say?
o: that the way is hard, and you're carrying a bundle you can't put down.
games.why: Farid says the dervish's door is hard, and he walks the world's way, carrying a bundle with nowhere to throw it.

practice: If you can, wash your hands and face first, slowly, as a way of arriving; then sit still and let your head bow a little, the chin dropping toward the chest.
When the mind wanders to its bundle, the list, the worry, notice it's on your head, and bow again. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.
